title: The US spent billions on border surveillance. Why can’t it catch people before they die?
gist: MIT Technology Review cross-referenced nearly 4,000 sets of migrant remains against nearly 600 US Customs and Border Protection surveillance towers and found more than 1,050 people died within tower range between 2015 and early 2026, including over 110 near Anduril's AI-enabled autonomous towers, with most deaths in locations terrain analysis shows were not blind spots. The reporting documents algorithmic false negatives, broken hardware, agent non-response and a 25-year measurement vacuum even as CBP prepares to spend $1 billion on roughly 1,500 more towers by 2034.

insights.claim: More than 1,050 people died within the advertised range of US border surveillance towers between 2015 and early 2026, with deaths recorded inside the range of nearly two-thirds of all towers analyzed — a pattern of system-wide rather than localized failure.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: The first quantified outcome measure for a multibillion-dollar program that has never been independently benchmarked; it reframes tower efficacy as an open question for appropriators.
insights.quote: We found deaths within the advertised range of nearly two-thirds of all the towers we analyzed.

insights.claim: More than 110 people have died since 2021 within range of Anduril's autonomous towers, among the most advanced systems deployed, so the failures cannot be dismissed as artifacts of legacy hardware.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Directly attacks the upgrade thesis that newer AI towers fix the problem — the strongest claim against continued sole-source expansion.

insights.claim: Somewhere between 500 and 700 people have died since 2015 near at least one Remote Video Surveillance System tower, with more than 250 of the roughly 300 RVSS towers analyzed having a death in range and over 150 deaths occurring within half a mile of a tower.

insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A near-universal failure rate across a single vendor's installed base is the cleanest vendor-level evidence in the dataset.

insights.claim: Officials who oversaw border security across the last four presidential administrations believed deaths near the virtual wall were exceedingly rare or nonexistent, and none could point to any comparable analysis the government had conducted itself.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Decision-makers were operating on a factually wrong prior for two decades — the definition of an information failure inside a procurement cycle.

insights.claim: In one stretch of New Mexico desert covered by three Anduril towers, 19 people died in a single year, five of them visible from the same tower nearest one man's body, and at four more AI towers a few miles west another 10 bodies were found that year all in locations with at least one clear tower view.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Clustered failures at named installations are what an internal audit would have caught immediately, showing how narrow the monitoring gap is.

insights.claim: The first generation of remotely operated border cameras put 200 towers along the southern border in eight years at a cost of more than $429 million, and the Remote Video Surveillance System program's total cost was estimated in 2020 at $3.7 billion.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Baseline for judging whether AI towers are cheaper per unit of coverage — the legacy program is the cost comparator.

insights.claim: General Dynamics won a 2013 contract worth up to $103 million to overhaul and expand the RVSS network, a ceiling that grew to $216 million, followed by another award worth up to $135 million in 2023.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Shows contract ceilings escalating roughly twofold over the base award — the pattern to expect on current AI tower vehicles.

insights.claim: Elbit won the integrated fixed tower program initially focused on Arizona, building 55 towers under an initial $145 million contract plus follow-ons, collectively watching more than 7,000 square miles.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Per-tower economics of roughly $2.6 million on the initial award set the reference point for radar-cued fixed towers.

insights.claim: Anduril moved from pilot to an official program of record in two years with its first hardware product, had over $98 million spent on it by June 2021, and its tower contract is now worth up to $1.1 billion.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A template for defense-tech entrants: SBIR grants to program of record at unusual speed, then a billion-dollar ceiling — the playbook rivals will copy.
insights.quote: That’s light speed in the world of government procurement, especially since it was Anduril’s first hardware product.

insights.claim: The government estimated in 2023 that its plans for the towers, now numbering 803, would cost $6.2 billion over their lifespan, and CBP plans to spend $1 billion for 1,497 more towers by 2034.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Lifecycle cost, not unit price, is where the money sits — sustainment contracts may be the larger prize than the build.

insights.claim: The government spending bill passed in July 2025 awarded $2.7 billion for border security technology alone, and CBP quickly signaled to industry in a webinar that the money would start flowing.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Near-term catalyst with a defined dollar figure and an agency actively courting vendors — the window for share shifts is now.

insights.claim: Anduril did not manufacture the cameras or radar in its towers, so its classification and tracking algorithms were its main value proposition to Border Patrol — a software moat wrapped around commodity sensors.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: If the moat is software on off-the-shelf hardware, it is replicable; watch whether competitors close the gap on detection quality.

insights.claim: General Dynamics has now released AI towers of its own and received a CBP order for them in June worth up to $115 million, with some already spotted at the border, ending Anduril's position as the only autonomous tower supplier.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: First credible competitive entry into the AI tower segment — margin and share pressure on the incumbent as the 2034 buildout ramps.

insights.claim: Anduril's standard tower is advertised at about 1.75 miles of range versus more than five miles for Elbit and General Dynamics models, with the company arguing automatic identification and tracking compensates; its newer 80-foot extended-range towers claim detection up to 7.5 miles.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: The tradeoff being sold is software range compression for automation — the extended-range product suggests the agency wanted both.

insights.claim: Anduril's towers have been sold abroad to enforce the UK's borders, defend US Marine Corps bases in Japan and elsewhere, and serve as drone defenses at an Australian Air Force base, with the founder saying in December 2025 that the towers remained the company's best-selling product.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Export and base-defense demand diversifies the revenue base away from CBP procurement risk — a key offset if US oversight tightens.

insights.so_what: Local political preference is shifting from physical wall to surveillance tech, which reallocates budget toward tower vendors regardless of federal posture.

insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A field-observed false-negative rate is the metric absent from every vendor release — use it as the benchmark to demand from competitors.

insights.claim: Smugglers defeated the classifier by covering up to a dozen people with a tarp on a rubber raft propelled by submersible motors; the system registered motion but labeled it an unidentified object, which suppressed the audible alert agents relied on, and the tactic was repeated dozens of times without being resolved.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A live example of adversarial evasion beating a fielded computer vision system and of retraining loops failing to close within a year — the durability risk in AI-led sensing.
insights.quote: The tarp fooled the algorithm, which detected the motion but attributed it only to an “unidentified object.”
insights.locator: Philip Sullivan worked as an agent in the Laredo sector too

insights.claim: Anduril has publicly emphasized reducing false positives such as mistaking wildlife for people, while saying little about false negatives — the people the systems fail to detect, which is the failure mode that correlates with deaths.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: The marketed metric and the safety-relevant metric are different; demand miss-rate disclosure before underwriting efficacy claims.
insights.locator: Anduril has touted its technology’s ability to reduce false positives

insights.claim: Because the autonomous towers constantly pan and linger only on an object of interest, agents found incidents were sometimes never captured at all, including a vehicle that crashed into the Rio Grande less than 100 feet from a tower with no footage recorded.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Continuous panning means coverage is temporal as well as spatial — advertised area coverage overstates real-world probability of capture.
insights.locator: Jaime Fierro, the former agent in the Laredo sector

insights.claim: Algorithm misclassification persisted in the field, with groups of people sometimes labeled as cattle so no alert was generated, and the error rate rising with distance from the camera.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Accuracy degrades with range, so effective coverage radius is materially smaller than advertised detection radius.
insights.locator: Reyes says algorithm mistakes were infrequent but problematic

insights.claim: Terrain collapses advertised coverage unevenly: topographical analysis estimated the El Paso sector's flat landscape gave towers 80% to 90% visibility, while Anduril towers in the mountainous Otay Mountain Wilderness could see just 15% to 25% of their promised coverage area, and some towers overall have sight of as little as 10% of their advertised surveillance area.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Coverage per dollar varies by nearly an order of magnitude with geography — siting, not hardware, drives realized capability.

insights.claim: Border Patrol says towers can hand off surveillance of people from one tower to another, but agents on the ground say people are often missed during those handoffs, and large groups that splinter while being pursued are not fully tracked.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Network-level tracking, not single-tower detection, is where the system breaks — a hard problem that more towers alone will not fix.

insights.claim: The chief of Border Patrol from June 2023 to March 2025 said the agency never reached the point of 'set it and forget it' with the tower algorithms, an admission that the autonomy premise remained unfulfilled through the newest generation.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Autonomy claims are not validated by the buyer's own leadership — a discount to apply to any labor-saving ROI model for these systems.

insights.claim: Hardware reliability remained a chronic problem: House Homeland Security Committee members wrote in 2024 that more than 66% of first-generation towers were unusable despite operating budgets of $50 million to $100 million a year, and a congressional staffer said 30% remained broken in January 2026.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Two-thirds unusable at peak, still a third broken two years later — sustainment failure is the quiet destroyer of coverage math.

insights.claim: The original design flaw was information overload: with up to 30 screens on a wall each covering three to five miles in any direction, one agent was expected to watch upwards of 850 square miles, and the former CBP tower program manager estimates the chance of noticing an event after 20 minutes at about zero.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A reusable constraint for evaluating any sensing buildout: detection capacity is bounded by attention, not by cameras.

insights.claim: Camera monitoring is the job nobody wants inside Border Patrol and is often assigned to injured agents, while at one New Mexico station agents responsible for 30 cameras also had to handle sensor alerts, radio traffic and records checks, monitoring cameras only if time remained.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Organizational incentives, not technology, determine whether surveillance output is consumed — a failure mode that survives every hardware upgrade.

insights.claim: Installing more towers increased rather than reduced staffing demand: while headquarters asked how many fewer agents they could get by with, supervisors receiving new towers asked for more agents because they now had more previously unseen activity to respond to.

insights.so_what: Kills the labor-substitution ROI case for surveillance tech — the same trap applies to enterprise AI monitoring deployments.

insights.claim: A distrust feedback loop emerged during rollout: an agent who saw a tower miss something significant would override the AI and operate the camera manually when it was their shift, which produced more missed alerts and further distrust.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Automation adoption fails through operator trust erosion, not only model error — a generalizable risk in any human-in-the-loop AI deployment.

insights.claim: Even after border encounters fell by 2024 to nearly one-tenth of their El Paso sector peak, freeing agents who had been tied up processing asylum claims, deaths near towers continued — so agent overload cannot explain all the failures found.

insights.so_what: The natural experiment inside the dataset: the same failure rate under both high and low load points to systemic design issues.

insights.claim: Agents described deliberately not responding to alerts as a tactic — hanging back to observe a group's route, ignoring small groups suspected of being decoys for larger ones, or waiting to intercept at a more practical location — meaning detection is routinely decoupled from intervention by design.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Alert-to-response conversion is a policy choice, not a capability limit, which complicates any efficacy metric based on detections.

insights.claim: Volunteers report giving Border Patrol coordinates for people who were lost but alive and waiting up to a week for agents to reach the location, by which time the people were remains.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Response latency measured in days, not minutes, is the operative failure even when location information is perfect.

insights.claim: Footage and data from the autonomous towers are overwritten every 30 days and are preserved only as part of an active investigation, which begins only if someone dies in custody, so no evidentiary record survives for deaths in the field.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Data retention policy determines what can ever be audited; changing it is the single cheapest oversight lever available to Congress.
insights.locator: We can’t know what those cameras saw as these people died

insights.claim: CBP does not formally investigate whether surveillance should have detected a person whose body is found, or why agents did not reach someone who was detected, and there is no procedure at local or national level to examine deaths near towers individually or collectively.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: No failure-review process means no learning loop, which is why identical failure modes recur across three technology generations.

insights.claim: Border enforcement metrics are constructed so no outcome can falsify the program: rising apprehensions are read as agents becoming more effective, and falling apprehensions as evidence the border is quiet because people are too scared to cross.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A reusable warning for any policy or product whose KPIs are bidirectionally self-justifying — it signals that effectiveness is unmeasured, not proven.

insights.claim: A 2014 GAO recommendation that agents log when technology assisted an apprehension was adopted but has repeatedly produced unreliable data, with agents treating the requirement as a chore demanded by bureaucrats, one former DHS official calling it 'spitting in the wind.'
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Twelve years of failed attribution data explains why Congress still cannot tell which surveillance systems work.

insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Displacement is the measurable second-order effect and the likely mechanism linking tower density to death density.

insights.so_what: The calibrated middle position: the systems work marginally, are sold as transformational, and the gap is where budget risk sits.

insights.claim: Border surveillance technology retains bipartisan support because hardliners see it as a tool against smugglers while others tout it as a cheaper alternative to a physical wall, which is why funding has surged despite the absence of efficacy data.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: The dual political rationale explains the durability of the spend and why efficacy findings are unlikely to slow it near term.

insights.claim: Rescue infrastructure has been a persistent weak point: CBP created a search and rescue unit in 1998 and had installed some 170 rescue beacons by August 2023, but a retired supervisor says people either avoid them or die next to them because agents cannot reach them in time, and one beacon's signal light was found switched off.
